question: Under Texas Property Code Section 5.021, a conveyance of a freehold estate or an estate for more than one year must satisfy which minimum requirements to be valid?
choice_a: It must be in writing and subscribed and delivered by the grantor or the grantor's agent authorized in writing
choice_b: It must be acknowledged before a notary and filed with the Texas Real Estate Commission
choice_c: It must be witnessed by two disinterested parties in addition to being signed
choice_d: It must state the exact purchase price paid by the grantee
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 5.021 requires that a conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold, or an estate for more than one year be in writing and be subscribed and delivered by the conveyor (or an agent authorized in writing) -- acknowledgment is needed for recording, not validity between the parties, and Texas does not require attesting witnesses for a deed to be valid.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 5.021 (requisites of a conveyance)

question: A grantor sells a ranch that she inherited from her uncle and executes a deed warranting title only against defects arising during her own period of ownership, making no promises about the property's history before she acquired it. This is a:
choice_a: Special warranty deed
choice_b: General warranty deed
choice_c: Quitclaim deed
choice_d: Deed of trust
explanation: A special warranty deed limits the grantor's warranty to defects arising during the grantor's own ownership of the property, offering less protection than a general warranty deed (which covers the entire chain of title) but more than a quitclaim deed (which offers no warranty at all).
source_note: Texas Property Code Ch. 5 (deed types and covenants); TREC broker curriculum on grantor warranties

question: A grantor signs a valid deed but locks it in a desk drawer, intending to hand it to the grantee only after receiving final payment next month. Before that happens, has a legally effective conveyance occurred?
choice_a: No, because delivery with present intent to convey is an essential element of a valid conveyance, separate from signing
choice_b: Yes, because signing alone completes the conveyance regardless of delivery
choice_c: Yes, because recording the deed is what completes the conveyance, not delivery
choice_d: No, because Texas requires the grantee's signature on the deed as well
explanation: A deed has no legal effect until it is delivered with the grantor's present intent that title pass immediately -- merely signing and retaining the instrument, with delivery deferred to a future event, does not transfer title until actual delivery and acceptance occur.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 5.021 (delivery requirement); general conveyancing doctrine

question: Which method of legal description is most commonly used to identify parcels of land in Texas deeds, as opposed to the rectangular government survey system used in many other states?
choice_a: Metes and bounds, often combined with lot-and-block references in platted subdivisions
choice_b: The federal township-and-range government survey system exclusively
choice_c: Street address alone
choice_d: Tax assessor parcel number alone, with no other description permitted
explanation: Because Texas was never surveyed under the federal rectangular (township-and-range) system, land in Texas is described chiefly by metes and bounds -- courses and distances tied to a point of beginning -- or, within recorded subdivisions, by lot and block reference to a filed plat.
source_note: Texas land survey history; Texas Property Code Sec. 11.001 et seq. (recording of plats)

question: After closing, the parties discover the recorded warranty deed contains a typographical error in the legal description that does not reflect the parties' actual agreement. The customary instrument used to fix this without a new sale is a:
choice_a: Correction deed executed to correct the clerical or scrivener's error in the original recorded conveyance
choice_b: Quitclaim deed reconveying the entire property back to the grantor
choice_c: New deed of trust naming a substitute trustee
choice_d: Notice of lis pendens filed against the property
explanation: Texas Property Code Chapter 5, Subchapter B allows a correction instrument (correction deed) to fix a clerical error, such as a typo in a legal description, without unwinding and re-executing the entire original conveyance.
source_note: Texas Property Code Ch. 5, Subchapter B (correction instruments)

question: An estate administrator conveys a decedent's property to a buyer using a deed that transfers only the interest the estate holds and includes no personal warranty of title from the administrator. This type of fiduciary deed is a(n):
choice_a: Executor's or administrator's deed
choice_b: General warranty deed
choice_c: Deed of trust
choice_d: Trustee's deed upon foreclosure
explanation: An executor's or administrator's deed is executed by a personal representative of an estate acting in a fiduciary capacity; because the representative has no personal stake in the property's title history, this deed customarily carries no personal warranty, binding only the estate's interest.
source_note: Texas Estates Code (personal representative's authority to convey); general conveyancing doctrine

question: A deed conveys land to a buyer 'on condition that the property never be used to sell alcohol; if it is, grantor reserves the right to reenter and terminate the estate.' Unlike a fee simple determinable, this fee simple subject to condition subsequent:
choice_a: Does not automatically terminate on breach -- the grantor must affirmatively exercise the right of reentry (power of termination) to end the estate
choice_b: Automatically reverts to the grantor the instant the condition is violated, with no action required
choice_c: Cannot be created by any deed language in Texas
choice_d: Converts automatically into a life estate upon breach of the condition
explanation: A fee simple subject to condition subsequent is created by conditional language (such as 'on condition that' or 'provided that') and, unlike a fee simple determinable's automatic reverter, requires the grantor to take affirmative legal action -- exercising the right of reentry, or power of termination -- to actually retake the property after breach.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.b (fee simple defeasible estates); Texas property law distinguishing determinable vs. condition subsequent estates

question: A grantor conveys a life estate to her brother but the deed names no one to take the property when the life estate ends. What happens to the property upon the brother's death?
choice_a: It reverts automatically to the grantor (or the grantor's heirs), an interest known as a reversion
choice_b: It escheats to the State of Texas because no remainderman was named
choice_c: It passes to the life tenant's heirs as if he owned a fee simple
choice_d: It becomes a fee simple determinable held by the county
explanation: When a grantor creates a life estate but does not name a third party to receive the property afterward, the grantor retains a reversion -- a future interest that brings the property back to the grantor or the grantor's heirs automatically when the life estate ends; this differs from a remainder, which sends the property to a named third party instead of back to the grantor.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.c (future interests -- remainder and reversion), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A deed grants a life estate to a caretaker 'for as long as my mother is living,' rather than measuring the estate by the caretaker's own life. This is an example of a life estate:
choice_a: Pur autre vie
choice_b: In fee tail
choice_c: At sufferance
choice_d: From period to period
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie ('for the life of another') is measured by the lifespan of someone other than the life tenant; the estate ends when that measuring life -- here, the mother -- dies, not when the life tenant dies.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.c (life estate variations -- pur autre vie), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A tenant occupies an apartment under an oral month-to-month agreement, with rent paid and accepted every month and no fixed ending date. This leasehold is a:
choice_a: Periodic tenancy (estate from period to period)
choice_b: Tenancy at will
choice_c: Tenancy at sufferance
choice_d: Estate for years
explanation: A periodic tenancy (estate from period to period) automatically renews for successive equal periods, such as month to month, until either party gives proper notice to terminate; it is distinguished from a tenancy at will, which has no set period and no expectation of automatic renewal.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.3.a (estate from period to period), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A property owner allows a friend to live in a spare house rent-free with no lease and no agreed duration, terminable by either party at any time. This possessory interest is a:
choice_a: Tenancy (estate) at will
choice_b: Periodic tenancy
choice_c: Estate for years
choice_d: Tenancy at sufferance
explanation: A tenancy (estate) at will exists only for as long as both parties agree to it, with no fixed term and no automatic renewal period, and may be terminated by either party at will -- distinct from a tenancy at sufferance, which involves a tenant remaining without the owner's continued consent.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.3.b (estate at will), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Under Texas Family Code Section 3.002, property acquired by either spouse during the marriage, other than that spouse's separate property, is classified as:
choice_a: Community property
choice_b: Joint tenancy property
choice_c: Tenancy in common property
choice_d: Homestead property
explanation: Texas Family Code Section 3.002 defines community property as the property, other than separate property, acquired by either spouse during the marriage -- Texas being one of a small number of community property states, this classification governs how marital real property is owned and must be conveyed.
source_note: Texas Family Code Sec. 3.002 (community property)

question: A spouse owned a house free and clear before marrying, and continues to hold title in her name alone after the wedding. Under Texas Family Code Section 3.001, this house remains her:
choice_a: Separate property, because it was owned by the spouse before marriage
choice_b: Community property, because all real estate owned during a marriage is automatically community property
choice_c: Homestead property owned jointly with her spouse regardless of when it was acquired
choice_d: Property held in a tenancy in common with her spouse by operation of law
explanation: Texas Family Code Section 3.001 defines a spouse's separate property to include property owned or claimed by the spouse before marriage; that character does not change simply because the owner later marries -- though homestead protections on the property may still apply to both spouses.
source_note: Texas Family Code Sec. 3.001 (separate property)

question: During the marriage, a spouse's uncle dies and leaves her a rental duplex by will. Under Texas Family Code Section 3.001, this inherited property is classified as:
choice_a: Her separate property, because property acquired during marriage by gift, devise, or descent is excluded from community property
choice_b: Community property, since it was acquired while married
choice_c: Jointly owned property requiring both spouses' names on title before it can be considered valid
choice_d: Property that automatically escheats to the state until probate closes
explanation: Even though acquired during the marriage, property received by gift, devise (through a will), or descent (through intestacy) is expressly carved out as separate property under Texas Family Code Section 3.001, rather than becoming community property simply because of the timing of acquisition.
source_note: Texas Family Code Sec. 3.001(2) (separate property -- gift, devise, or descent)

question: A married person is injured in a car accident during the marriage and recovers a settlement. Under Texas Family Code Section 3.001, which portion of that recovery is treated as community property rather than the injured spouse's separate property?
choice_a: The portion of the recovery attributable to loss of earning capacity during the marriage
choice_b: The entire recovery, without exception
choice_c: None of the recovery -- personal injury settlements are always fully separate property
choice_d: Only the portion attributable to pain and suffering
explanation: Texas Family Code Section 3.001 makes a personal injury recovery a spouse's separate property, but carves out one exception: the portion of the recovery compensating for loss of earning capacity during the marriage remains community property, since lost wages during marriage would otherwise have been community income.
source_note: Texas Family Code Sec. 3.001(3) (separate property -- personal injury recovery exception)

question: In a Texas divorce or probate dispute, property possessed by either spouse during the marriage is presumed to be community property. Under Texas Family Code Section 3.003, what standard of proof must a spouse meet to establish that specific property is actually separate property?
choice_a: Clear and convincing evidence
choice_b: A mere preponderance of the evidence
choice_c: Beyond a reasonable doubt
choice_d: No evidence is required; a spouse's sworn assertion alone is conclusive
explanation: Texas Family Code Section 3.003 creates a presumption that property possessed by either spouse during or on dissolution of marriage is community property, and requires the higher standard of clear and convincing evidence -- not the ordinary civil preponderance standard -- to rebut that presumption and establish separate property status.
source_note: Texas Family Code Sec. 3.003 (presumption of community property)

question: A husband holds title to the family's homestead in his name alone as his separate property, acquired before marriage. Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50(b), can he sell or convey the homestead without his wife joining in the deed?
choice_a: No -- neither spouse may sell, convey, or encumber the homestead without the other spouse's consent, regardless of whose separate property it is
choice_b: Yes, because it is his separate property and his wife has no legal interest requiring her signature
choice_c: Yes, but only if the couple has been married less than one year
choice_d: No, but only if the property is rural rather than urban
explanation: Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50(b) prohibits selling, conveying, or encumbering homestead property without the consent of both spouses, regardless of whether the property is separate or community -- a protection unique to homestead status that does not depend on how title is actually held.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(b) (spousal consent to sell or encumber homestead)

question: Two spouses want to ensure that when one of them dies, the surviving spouse automatically owns their community property real estate outright, without probate. Under Texas Estates Code Chapter 112, merely titling the deed 'as joint tenants' is:
choice_a: Insufficient -- a valid right-of-survivorship agreement for community property must be in writing and signed by both spouses
choice_b: Sufficient by itself to create a binding right of survivorship in community property
choice_c: Prohibited entirely, since Texas does not recognize any survivorship arrangement for community property
choice_d: Only effective if recorded within 30 days of the marriage
explanation: Texas Estates Code Section 112.052 requires that a community property survivorship agreement between spouses be in writing and signed by both spouses; joint account or title designations such as 'JT TEN' or 'joint tenancy' standing alone do not, by themselves, create a valid right of survivorship in community property.
source_note: Texas Estates Code Sec. 112.051-112.052 (community property survivorship agreements)

question: Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50, what is the maximum acreage that can be claimed as an urban homestead?
choice_a: 10 acres, which may be in one or more contiguous lots, together with any improvements
choice_b: 1 acre
choice_c: 100 acres
choice_d: 200 acres
explanation: Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50 limits an urban homestead to 10 acres, which may consist of one or more contiguous lots together with any improvements on them, regardless of whether the claimant is a family or a single adult.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a) (urban homestead -- 10-acre limit)

question: A married couple owns and farms land outside any city or town. Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50, what is the maximum acreage they may claim as a rural family homestead?
choice_a: 200 acres
choice_b: 100 acres
choice_c: 10 acres
choice_d: There is no acreage limit for a rural family homestead
explanation: Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50 allows a family claiming a rural homestead to protect up to 200 acres, which may be in one or more parcels, along with the improvements on it -- double the 100-acre limit that applies to a rural homestead claimed by a single adult person.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a) (rural homestead -- 200-acre family limit)

question: An unmarried adult who lives alone farms land outside any city or town and wants to claim it as a homestead. Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50, what is the maximum rural acreage this single adult may claim?
choice_a: 100 acres
choice_b: 200 acres
choice_c: 10 acres
choice_d: 50 acres
explanation: Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50 sets the rural homestead limit at 100 acres for a single adult person not constituting a family, in contrast to the 200-acre limit available to a family claiming a rural homestead.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a) (rural homestead -- 100-acre single-adult limit)

question: A Texas homeowner who financed the purchase of her homestead with a loan secured by that same purchase later defaults. Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50, can the lender foreclose despite the property's homestead status?
choice_a: Yes -- a purchase-money lien is one of the specific categories of debt for which a homestead can be validly encumbered and foreclosed
choice_b: No -- homestead status bars foreclosure on any debt whatsoever, including the original purchase loan
choice_c: Only if the homeowner is single and childless
choice_d: Only if the lender first obtains a judgment through a jury trial
explanation: While Texas homestead protection generally shields the property from forced sale for ordinary debts, Article XVI, Section 50 expressly lists narrow exceptions -- including purchase-money liens, ad valorem property taxes, home improvement liens, owelty of partition, and certain home equity loans -- for which a valid lien and foreclosure can still reach the homestead.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a)(1) (purchase-money exception to homestead protection)

question: A licensed contractor performs unpaid, contracted improvements directly on a Texas homeowner's homestead. Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50, can the contractor's lien for that work validly attach to and be foreclosed against the homestead?
choice_a: Yes -- a valid mechanic's, materialman's, or home improvement lien for work contracted for in writing before the work begins is a recognized exception to homestead protection
choice_b: No -- homestead status makes it legally impossible for any contractor to place a lien on the property
choice_c: Only if the contractor first obtains a judgment from a jury
choice_d: Only if the work was performed more than 200 miles from an urban area
explanation: Article XVI, Section 50 permits a valid lien for work and material used to construct improvements on a homestead, provided the required contract is executed and other constitutional formalities (such as written consent before work begins) are satisfied -- making home improvement liens one of the enumerated exceptions to the general homestead protection from forced sale.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a)(5) (home improvement/mechanic's lien exception)

question: Beyond a purchase-money mortgage, property taxes, and mechanic's liens, Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50(a)(6) creates a special, heavily regulated category of lending secured by a homestead known as a(n):
choice_a: Home equity loan
choice_b: Unsecured personal line of credit
choice_c: Reverse annuity contract with no lien rights
choice_d: General judgment lien
explanation: Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 50(a)(6) authorizes home equity lending against a homestead, subject to unique constitutional safeguards not required for other mortgages, including limits on the amount that can be borrowed relative to the home's fair market value and a closing that cannot occur less than a set number of days after application.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a)(6) (home equity lending)

question: A creditor obtains a routine money judgment against a Texas homeowner for an unpaid, unsecured credit card debt unrelated to the property. Can that judgment creditor force the sale of the homeowner's homestead to satisfy the debt?
choice_a: No -- a general, unsecured judgment lien does not attach to and cannot force the sale of a properly claimed Texas homestead
choice_b: Yes, any money judgment automatically becomes enforceable against a homestead once recorded
choice_c: Yes, but only if the debt exceeds $10,000
choice_d: Yes, but only if the homeowner is unmarried
explanation: One of the core purposes of the Texas homestead exemption is to shield a family's home from forced sale for ordinary unsecured debts; a general judgment lien from routine litigation does not attach to homestead property, unlike the narrow list of debts (purchase money, taxes, mechanic's liens, home equity loans, and similar) that the constitution specifically allows to reach it.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 50(a) (homestead protection from forced sale for general debts)

question: A Texas deed-of-trust lender wants to foreclose on a defaulted borrower's property without going through a court lawsuit. Under Texas Property Code Section 51.002, how many days' notice of the foreclosure sale itself must be given before the sale date?
choice_a: At least 21 days
choice_b: At least 90 days
choice_c: At least 3 days
choice_d: At least 60 days
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 51.002 requires that notice of a non-judicial foreclosure sale be given at least 21 days before the date of sale, through posting, filing, and mailing -- one of the key statutory deadlines governing Texas's streamlined power-of-sale foreclosure process under a deed of trust.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 51.002(b) (21-day notice of foreclosure sale)

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 51.002, which of the following combinations correctly describes how notice of a non-judicial foreclosure sale must be given?
choice_a: Posted at the courthouse door of each county where the property is located, filed with that county's county clerk, and mailed by certified mail to each debtor obligated on the debt
choice_b: Published once in a national newspaper only, with no requirement to notify the debtor directly
choice_c: Delivered only by a process server hand-delivering notice to the debtor
choice_d: Emailed to the debtor's last known email address, with no posting or filing required
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 51.002(b) requires the trustee (or substitute trustee) to give notice of sale through three simultaneous channels: posting at the county courthouse door, filing with the county clerk, and mailing by certified mail to each debtor who is obligated to pay the underlying debt.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 51.002(b) (notice methods -- posting, filing, and certified mail)

question: Under Texas Property Code Section 51.002, a non-judicial foreclosure sale of real property under a power of sale must generally occur:
choice_a: Between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of the month
choice_b: At any time on the last business day of the month
choice_c: Only on the first Monday of the month between 8 a.m. and noon
choice_d: Only during a special legislative foreclosure session
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 51.002 requires that a foreclosure sale under a power of sale in a deed of trust be conducted between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of the month (shifting to the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday falls on January 1 or July 4), at the county courthouse or another designated public location.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 51.002(a) (first-Tuesday foreclosure sale timing)

question: Before a mortgage servicer can even give notice of a Texas foreclosure sale, Texas Property Code Section 51.002 requires that the borrower first be given written notice of default and how many days to cure it?
choice_a: At least 20 days
choice_b: At least 60 days
choice_c: At least 5 days
choice_d: No cure period is required before notice of sale
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 51.002(d) requires the mortgage servicer to serve the debtor with written notice by certified mail that the debtor is in default, giving the debtor at least 20 days to cure the default before a notice of sale may be given -- a separate and earlier deadline from the later 21-day notice of the sale itself.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 51.002(d) (20-day notice of default and right to cure)

question: Compared to a judicial foreclosure, the non-judicial foreclosure process used under a Texas deed of trust is faster primarily because it:
choice_a: Does not require the lender to file a lawsuit or obtain a court judgment before the trustee can sell the property under the power of sale
choice_b: Eliminates any notice requirement to the defaulting borrower
choice_c: Can be completed the same day a single missed payment occurs
choice_d: Requires approval from the Texas Real Estate Commission before each sale
explanation: Because a deed of trust grants the trustee a contractual power of sale, a lender can foreclose by satisfying the statutory notice and timing requirements of Property Code Section 51.002 without filing suit or obtaining a court judgment first, unlike a judicial foreclosure, which requires a full lawsuit and court decree.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 51.002 (power-of-sale non-judicial foreclosure vs. judicial foreclosure)

question: A buyer purchases property for value, has no actual or constructive notice of a prior unrecorded deed to someone else, and records her own deed first. Under Texas Property Code Section 13.001, whose interest generally prevails?
choice_a: The subsequent bona fide purchaser who recorded first without notice of the earlier unrecorded conveyance
choice_b: The earlier grantee, automatically, regardless of recording, because the earlier deed was executed first in time
choice_c: Neither party -- the property automatically escheats to the state when a recording conflict arises
choice_d: Whichever party paid the higher purchase price
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 13.001 makes an unrecorded conveyance void as to a later, good-faith purchaser for valuable consideration who has no notice of it and who records first, reflecting Texas's race-notice approach to recording priority and underscoring why prompt recording matters even between innocent parties.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 13.001 (validity of unrecorded instrument as to subsequent purchasers)

question: Under Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.024, a person seeking to recover real property from someone who has held it in peaceable and adverse possession under title or color of title must sue within:
choice_a: 3 years from when the cause of action accrues
choice_b: 5 years from when the cause of action accrues
choice_c: 10 years from when the cause of action accrues
choice_d: 25 years from when the cause of action accrues
explanation: Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.024 sets a 3-year limitations period for recovering real property held by another in peaceable and adverse possession when that possessor holds title or color of title -- the shortest of Texas's several adverse possession limitations periods, precisely because the possessor already has some documented claim to title.
source_note: Texas Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code Sec. 16.024 (3-year adverse possession -- title or color of title)

question: Under Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.025, a claimant seeking to establish adverse possession under this 5-year statute must show possession under a duly registered deed plus which additional elements?
choice_a: Cultivation, use, or enjoyment of the property, and payment of applicable taxes on it
choice_b: A notarized affidavit filed annually with TREC
choice_c: Possession under a quitclaim deed specifically
choice_d: Continuous residence for at least 25 consecutive years
explanation: Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.025 requires a claimant asserting the 5-year adverse possession statute to hold under a duly registered deed while cultivating, using, or enjoying the property and paying the applicable taxes on it; the statute expressly does not apply to claims resting on a quitclaim deed, a forged deed, or a deed executed under a forged power of attorney.
source_note: Texas Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code Sec. 16.025 (5-year adverse possession -- registered deed, use, and tax payment)

question: A rancher fences and continuously farms a strip of adjoining land for over a decade without ever holding any deed or color of title to it. Under Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.026, this longer 10-year adverse possession claim generally:
choice_a: Does not require title or color of title, but is limited to a defined acreage unless the possessor's claim is by actual enclosure of a larger tract
choice_b: Requires the same duly registered deed that the 5-year statute requires
choice_c: Is unavailable in Texas under any circumstances
choice_d: Automatically grants title to an unlimited amount of adjoining acreage
explanation: Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 16.026 allows adverse possession after 10 years of cultivation, use, or enjoyment without any deed or color of title, but caps the claim's acreage unless the possession is by actual enclosure -- distinguishing it from the 5-year statute, which requires a registered deed but no acreage cap.
source_note: Texas Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code Sec. 16.026 (10-year adverse possession -- no title required, acreage limited)

question: Compared to a private mortgage lien recorded years earlier, how does a Texas ad valorem property tax lien generally rank in priority against the property?
choice_a: The tax lien has priority over essentially all other liens, including a pre-existing recorded mortgage
choice_b: The tax lien is always subordinate to any mortgage recorded before the taxes became due
choice_c: Tax liens and mortgage liens are paid on a strict pro-rata basis regardless of recording date
choice_d: Property taxes create no lien on real property in Texas
explanation: Ad valorem property tax liens in Texas attach automatically and carry superior priority over virtually all other liens and encumbrances against the property, including previously recorded mortgages -- which is why lenders typically require escrowed tax payments to protect their own lien position.
source_note: Texas Tax Code (property tax lien priority); Texas Property Code Sec. 32.005 (tax lien)

question: Under Texas Constitution Article XVI, Section 37, contractors, artisans, and material suppliers who furnish labor or materials to construct or repair a building are automatically given what protection, independent of any contract clause?
choice_a: A constitutional mechanic's and materialman's lien on the structure for the value of their labor or materials
choice_b: Automatic co-ownership of the finished building
choice_c: The right to demand a jury trial before any construction begins
choice_d: Immunity from any claims arising out of the construction contract
explanation: Texas is unusual in that Article XVI, Section 37 of its constitution grants mechanics, artisans, and material suppliers a lien on the structures they build or repair for the value of their labor and materials -- a self-executing constitutional right that exists independent of, and in addition to, any statutory lien procedures.
source_note: Texas Constitution Art. XVI, Sec. 37 (constitutional mechanic's and materialman's lien)

question: A creditor wins a lawsuit against a Texas property owner and records an abstract of judgment in the county where the owner's non-homestead rental property is located. What is the legal effect of that recorded abstract?
choice_a: It creates a general judgment lien attaching to the debtor's non-exempt real property in that county
choice_b: It automatically transfers title to the rental property to the creditor
choice_c: It has no legal effect until the debtor's homestead is also seized
choice_d: It creates a specific lien limited only to the exact property named in the lawsuit
explanation: Recording a properly issued abstract of judgment in a county creates a general judgment lien that attaches to all of the debtor's non-exempt real property located in that county -- including after-acquired property -- but, unlike a mortgage or mechanic's lien, this general lien does not reach a debtor's protected homestead.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 52.001 (abstract of judgment as a general lien)

question: Two unrelated business partners buy an investment property together in Texas, taking title without specifying any right of survivorship. Absent such language, Texas law presumes they hold title as:
choice_a: Tenants in common, each owning an undivided interest that passes to their own heirs, not automatically to the other co-owner, upon death
choice_b: Joint tenants with automatic right of survivorship
choice_c: Community property, regardless of marital status
choice_d: A general partnership that automatically dissolves title to the individual with the larger down payment
explanation: In Texas, co-owners who are not married to each other are presumed to hold title as tenants in common unless a valid, express right-of-survivorship agreement is created; each tenant in common owns an undivided fractional interest that can be sold, encumbered, or devised independently and passes to that co-owner's own heirs or estate, not automatically to the surviving co-owner.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sec. 5.001 (tenancy in common presumption); Texas Estates Code Ch. 111 (survivorship agreements between non-spouses)

question: A condominium buyer in Texas purchases Unit 204 in a building governed by the Texas Uniform Condominium Act. In addition to owning that individual unit, the buyer also automatically acquires:
choice_a: An undivided interest in the building's common elements, such as hallways, the roof, and shared structural components
choice_b: Exclusive ownership of the entire building, including every other unit
choice_c: A leasehold interest only, with the condominium association retaining fee title to the unit
choice_d: No interest in any shared areas of the building whatsoever
explanation: Condominium ownership under the Texas Uniform Condominium Act combines fee simple (or another estate) ownership of an individually described unit with an undivided percentage interest, shared with the other unit owners, in the building's common elements, such as shared walls, hallways, the roof, and structural systems.
source_note: Texas Uniform Condominium Act, Texas Property Code Ch. 82 (unit and common element ownership)

question: A Texas landowner sells the surface rights to a farm but retains the underlying oil and gas rights, which she later leases to an energy company. Under Texas law, when the mineral estate has been severed from the surface estate in this way, the mineral estate is generally treated as the:
choice_a: Dominant estate, carrying an implied right to use as much of the surface as reasonably necessary to explore for and produce the minerals
choice_b: Subordinate estate, with no right to access the surface without the surface owner's consent under any circumstance
choice_c: Same estate as the surface, since Texas does not allow severance of mineral rights from surface rights
choice_d: Estate that automatically terminates once the surface is sold to a new owner
explanation: Under longstanding Texas oil and gas law, once the mineral estate is severed from the surface estate, the mineral estate is treated as the dominant estate, carrying an implied right to use as much of the surface as is reasonably necessary to explore for, develop, and produce the minerals, subject to the accommodation doctrine limiting unreasonable interference with existing surface uses.
source_note: Texas oil and gas law -- dominant mineral estate doctrine and accommodation doctrine

question: A Texas landowner pumps groundwater from a well on her property for irrigation, even though the pumping measurably lowers the water table beneath a neighboring landowner's well. Under Texas's traditional 'rule of capture' for groundwater, the landowner:
choice_a: Generally may capture groundwater beneath her own land, even if doing so draws down groundwater beneath a neighbor's property, subject to regulation by local groundwater conservation districts
choice_b: Automatically owns the state-permitted right to that water the same way surface water rights are allocated
choice_c: Commits an automatic trespass any time pumping affects a neighboring well
choice_d: May never pump groundwater without a state-issued permit under any circumstances
explanation: Texas is one of the few states still following the common-law rule of capture for groundwater, under which a landowner generally has the right to capture and use groundwater beneath her own land -- even if that pumping affects a neighbor's well -- subject to reasonable regulation imposed by local groundwater conservation districts, in contrast to surface water, which the state owns and allocates through a permit system.
source_note: Texas groundwater law -- rule of capture (Houston & T.C. Ry. Co. v. East); contrast with state-owned, permitted surface water

question: Unlike groundwater, the water flowing in a natural Texas river or stream is legally treated as:
choice_a: Property of the State of Texas, allocated to users through a permit system administered by the state rather than owned outright by adjoining landowners
choice_b: The automatic private property of whoever owns the riverbank
choice_c: Unregulated and available for unlimited private diversion by any adjoining owner
choice_d: Subject to the same rule of capture that governs groundwater
explanation: In contrast to groundwater, which Texas treats under the rule of capture as belonging to the overlying landowner, surface water in Texas's natural rivers and streams is considered property of the state and is allocated to users through a permit system administered by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, based on a system of appropriative water rights.
source_note: Texas Water Code Sec. 11.021 (state ownership of surface water); TCEQ water rights permitting
